la:verb:sibilo.html:
sībĭlo (collat. form sīfĭlo, ), āre, v. n. and a.
[sibilus] (class. but rare).
Neutr., to hiss, to whistle: imitationis hoc modo, ut majores rudere et vagire et mugire et murmurare et sibilare appellaverunt,: (serpens) sibilat ore, * ; so of a serpent, Ov M. 4, 588.—Of gossips: contemplent, conspiciant omnes, nutent, nictent, sibilent, * .—Of things: illud (ferrum igne rubens) Stridet et in trepidā submersum sibilat undā,: stridor rudentum sibilat,whistles,; cf. aura,: tempestas,: horrendo fragore sibilantibus armis,.—
Act., to hiss, i. e. to hiss at, hiss down a person, : populus me sibilat; at mihi plaudo Ipse domi,.

la:noun:sibilus.html:
sībĭlus, i (collat. form, abl., sibilu, Sisenn. ap. P.—In plur. in the poets, prob. merely for the sake of the metre: sībĭla, ōrum; cf. 2. sibilus
init.; but in Cic. sibili), m.
cf. σιφνός, σιβλός, hollow; Angl. S. and Engl. sipan, sip; O. H. Germ. sip, Germ. Sieb, a sieve; regarded by the ancients as imitation of a natural sound; cf. ;
, a hissing, a whistling (class.)
In gen.
Sing., of men: sibilo dare signum,—Of cattle: (boves) sibilo allectari,.—Of things: clamor tonitruum et rudentum sibilus, Poët. ap. : (arbor) Loquente saepe sibilum edidit coma,: venientis sibilus austri,: sibilu significare alicui, Sisenn. ap. P.—
Plur., of wind instruments: calamorum sibila,; cf. pastoria,; .—Of snakes, etc.: serpens horrenda sibila misit,: sibila dant,: mittere,; 15, 684: sibila torsit draco,: angues stridula fuderunt vibratis sibila linguis,: sibila effundere,: vibrare,; Corn. Sev. and Macer ap. P.—Of a flying missile: stridentis sibila teli,; . —
In partic., a contemptuous hissing, a hissing at or off (usually in plur.).
Sing.: sibilum metuis?.—
Plur.: e scaenā sibilis explodi,: aliquem sibilis consectari,: crebris totius contionis sibilis vexatus,ext.; ; cf.: gladiatorii sibili, id. Fragm. ap. P.: quā dominus, quā advocati sibilis conscissi,.

la:noun:Sibylla.html:
Sĭbylla (in many MSS. and edd. Sĭbul-la, e. g. Ritter), ae, f.,= Σίβυλλα,
a female soothsayer, a prophetess, Sibyl, Varr. ap. ; , 18, 23; ; : has (litteras), credo, nisi Sibylla legerit, Interpretari alium potesse neminem,: terrae vis Pythiam Delphis incitabat: naturae Sibyllam. ; cf. .—In Roman mythology, the most celebrated is the Sibyl at Cumae, in the service of Apollo; in the time of Æneas,; ; ; ; .—A later Sibyl in the time of Tarquinius Superbus, whose predictions were deposited in the Capitol, and in time of danger were consulted by a college of priests, appointed for that special purpose (at first duumviri, afterwards decemviri and quindecemviri, v. h. vv.), ; sqq.; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; .—A later Sibyl, burnt by Stilicho, ; cf. Becker, Antiq. 4, p. 49 sq.—Hence, Sĭ-byllīnus (written SIBVLLIN., , and Calend. Praenest. M. Apr. ib. tom. ii. p. 389), a, um, adj., of or belonging to the Sibyl, Sibylline: libri, Varr. l. l.; Gell. l. l.; Müll.; ; ; ; ; 29, 10; 36, 37; 41, 21 al. (they are called simply libri in ; ; ; 22, 36; 22, 57; and libri fatales,): vaticinationes,: versus,; : fata,.
